reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This is an interesting manuscript demonstrating a mechanism underlying inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and bone
formation in idiopathic short stature (ISS) via miR-17-3p and plasma exosomes. The authors also show that a capsaicin-
supplemented diet reproduces features of the ISS phenotype in rats and provide a comprehensive set of experiments to
support their conclusions. Below, are some general and specific comments for consideration.
General comments
The authors report having developed a capsaicin dietary model. Though, the development and validation of the model are
not described. Line 749 refers to 0.01% of capsaicin-supplemented diet. It is unclear how this dose was selected and how it
represents physiologically relevant intakes (including in regions of the world with high consumption). Was it adjusted by rat
body weight to reflect intakes in humans? The source of capsaicin, and diets composition should be provided to allow
reproducibility. The response to previous reviewers speaks of various doses of capsaicin having been tested, though the
process should be described in the methods section of this paper. Also, the methodology should indicate that body weight
and food intake were assessed, and data shown. This is a nutritional study, and information on the diet composition and
form, source, mode of administration, housing (how many animals per cage? Sex?), sample size must be provided. Was the
capsaicin diet palatable for the mice? Was the capsaicin content of the diet confirmed? How does the amount of capsaicin
used in this study relates to studies in the literature, where this compound has beneficial effects including in conditions
associated with altered intestinal barrier function? Finally, because the age of the rats is not provided, it is difficult to relate
the dietary study and intestinal outcomes to the experiments on miR-17-3p inhibition of growth plate ossification.
Critical details are missing or are unclear in the methods section; examples are provided below.
This is a dense and impressive manuscript, and the authors should be commended for undertaking such a comprehensive
series of experiments. The data presented are valuable, and the overall effort is clear. That said, some sections are
challenging to follow. The manuscript could be improved by using more specific and consistent terminology, which would
greatly enhance clarity. At times, it was necessary to refer repeatedly to the Methods section to determine key details, for
example the specific cell line or intestinal tissue used, and occasionally, this information was not clearly stated even there.
Providing these details more explicitly in the main text and ensuring they are clearly outlined in the Methods would
strengthen the manuscript and improve its accessibility to readers.
Intestinal cell line experiments: these are hard to assess without knowing which intestinal cell line was used and the
culturing conditions. Also, there seems to be a confusion between viability and proliferation (for ex, see Supplementary Fig
15); these are not the same. Did the authors assess viability (ie using Trypan Blue exclusion or MTT) and used viable cells
for their experiments? Panel A shows viability % but the legend speaks of proliferation, please clarify. The fact that cell
viability was at most about 2.5% for 25 μM is concerning. This is important for this part of the manuscript because the authors
discuss that capsaicin effects (beneficial vs detrimental) depend on low vs high dosages. It is thus important to determine if
the 200 μM dosage is a usable high dosage or if it is ”toxic” to the cells. Experiments are hard to assess without details on
which intestinal cell line was used, culture conditions, and measures of viability and proliferation (Suppl Fig 15). Similarly to
the in vivo experiment, is 200 μM a physiologically relevant high concentration of capsaicin? Can it be reached in the diet? 
For example, a calculation of the amount of chili peppers that one should eat (on average) to reach this amount should be
provided.
Specific comments.
Abstract and Introduction
1. Abstract line 40: it is unclear why it necessary to specify: “different from inflammatory bowel disease”. IBD does not always
come with diarrhea. The authors did not compare the inflammatory profile induced by capsaicin with the IBD inflammatory
phenotype so this sentence should be revised.
2. Line 41: intestinal secretions: are the authors referring to intestinal content? In which intestinal region? It would be best to
just specify it.
3. Introduction: the authors could consider making this section more concise without describing all the details of their
findings already in this section.
4. Line 75: at which age and sex was this height gain assessed?
5. Line 127-128: dietary patterns are more than one ingredient, please rephrase: “frequent consumption of a capsaicin-rich
diet, mirroring dietary patterns….”; also, the authors could clarify what is meant by “frequent” and “capsaicin-rich”; It would be
helpful to know the amount of capsaicin in this diet to better understand the dosage used in the animal model.
Methods:
1. The term “pairs” used to describe ISS patients and age- and gender-matched controls (line 519, line 530) is misleading,
as those children are unrelated. Furthermore, the gender distribution between the two groups is different (NC: 57 males and
49 females, ISS: 52 males, 54 females), which indicate that not all “pairs” can be gender matched. Please revise
accordingly.
2. Fecal sample collection: The methods used to collect and preserve fecal samples from ISS and control children are not
described, please include this information in the clinical sample characteristics section.
3. Inconsistent microRNA methodology: The methods regarding microRNA profiling lack clarity. Line 535 mentions miRNA
High-Throughput Sequencing, while line 531 mentions miRNA microarray. Please clarify which method was used and
include appropriate method details (sequencing platform used, library preparation protocol, sequencing depth; or microarray
platform, miRNA labelling and amplification kit, number of miRNA analyzed).
4. 615-620: this paragraph is unclear regarding whether the experiment was conducted in immature mice, or in rats.
5. microRNA RT-qPCR: Line 623 does not specify which internal controls were used for 2-DeltaCt method of miRNA RT-
qPCR for plasma and stool samples. Please include this information.
6. The description of the in vivo models is incomplete, please ensure that the ARRIVE guidelines are followed; for example:
- Rats strains and age are missing in a few sections of the in vivo methods description (line 682, line 692, line 748).
- Grouping Figure: the supplementary Figure 27 and 28 (Grouping of experimental animals) seem to have been mislabeled or
switched with Supplementary Figure 24 or 25 (overexpression vector mapping) as the legend does not match the figure
content.
- Please provide justifications for the sample sizes used in the animal studies. Is n=3 sufficient?
- Please clarify which tissues were studied in the various experiments; terms like “intestinal tissues” are too vague, please
specify which regions.
7. More details are needed regarding the diets used in the in vivo studies. For example, what constitutes a ‘mixed diet’ (line
683) and a ‘regular diet’ (line 748). Is this the AIN-93 diet? How was the capsaicin-supplemented diet formulated, how does it differ from the group A ‘regular diet’, and how does the capsaicin dosage relate to human consumption?
8. The explant culture of rat femurs appears to have used samples collected at one day postpartum (line 708), indicating
neonatal rather than fetal samples. Please revise the terminology accordingly in the manuscript.
9. Histopathological analysis of the intestine: please specify which part of the small intestine or large intestine were used to
assess intestinal inflammation in rats. The method section mentions colon (line 754) while the figures refer to the small
intestine (line 1280). Please add details on the number of measurements conducted and samples size used to assess villus
height and intestinal wall thickness.
10. Line 757: “Cells were treated…”: Please clarify which cells and explain how they were cultured. How many times were
the cell culture experiments repeated? And were they done in triplicates or else?
11. Line 761-762: was the quality of the RNA assessed?
12. Line 763-767. Please specify use of parametric and non-parametric tests for data analysis based on data distribution.
Results
1. Please ensure that sample sizes are clarified in all figures and legends.
2. Body weight data missing: a decrease in body height was observed in immature rats fed a capsaicin diet compared to
controls, but the manuscript does not report their body weight. Since intestinal inflammation can lead to weight loss, please
include body weight data to support the interpretation of the growth findings.
3. Supplementary Figure 1a: the dendrogram on top (sample-based, rather than miRNA-based) should be shown to support
the statement in the text.
4. Supplementary Figure 1c: unclear what does the Y axis show, is this a Delta Ct or a fold change (and if so, please explain
versus what it was calculated). Please explain in legend.
5. Line 172: GO and KEGG pathway analyses indicated that overexpression of miR-17-3p upregulates the PI3K-akt etc”: a
KEGG or GO analysis can indicate that genes targeted by miR-17-3p are enriched in these pathways, not that the pathways
themselves are upregulated: please edit.
6. Line 245: immature rats: please clarify what is it meant by this
7. Supplementary Fig 14: the panels H and I seem to be switched, please also fix the corresponding text to match the
revised figure (line 265). Please clarify which intestinal tissues were studied (rather than saying: intestinal tissues) and also
clarify if you used whole thickness or the epithelial lining. What was the expression of the miR in Supplem Fig 14 relative to?
8. Lines 267-274. Please specify the cell line in the text (instead of “mucosal epithelial cells”). The authors seem to have
conducted a regular “dose-response” experiment of capsaicin at different dosages, which is routine good practice in cell
culture. It would be expected that at higher concentrations, the substance studied (here capsaicin) would inhibit cell viability,
which is why these experiments are usually performed to find the concentrations range to be studied. Is this what the authors
did? Was cell viability assessed? If so, how? How was the optimal concentration (line 270) defined, and which one is it?
9. Line 269: Supplem Fig 15 presents data on viability but not on proliferation as mentioned in the text.
Discussion
The discussion is well thought and clear.
Line 366: the SOS1 abbreviation should have been explained earlier in the manuscript.
Line 385: please provide a reference for “high chili pepper consumption”
Lines 396-400: this part of the discussion is important. It could be improved by relating it to the published dietary amounts of
dietary capsaicin showing beneficial effects. How do the concentrations used with the intestinal cell lines relate to dietary
intake in high and normal capsaicin-diets and to the amount of capsaicin known to elicit beneficial effects in published
animal studies? And then versus human intake.
Line 398: please clarify where the data on proliferation are presented. Please make sure that the discussion reflects the
results and that these are all presented.
Lines 431-432: we cannot find the data on mice with ulcerative colitis.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Reviewers,
We are deeply grateful for your thorough and insightful reviews of our manuscript, titled
"Capsaicin Diet-Induced Gut Inflammation Elevates Plasma Exosomal miR-17-3p: Unveiling the
ZNF148/SOS1 Axis as a Novel Mechanism in ISS Pathogenesis and Potential Therapeutic Target"
(Manuscript Number: NCOMMS-24-73070). Your valuable feedback has greatly enhanced the
clarity, rigor, and scientific impact of our work. We have carefully addressed each comment,
incorporating revisions to improve the manuscript’s quality and accessibility. For your
convenience, all revised sections in the manuscript are marked in blue. Below, we provide detailed
responses to each reviewer’s comments, including the changes made, their rationale, and relevant
line numbers in the revised manuscript.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The relationship of miR-17-3p/ZNF148/SOS1 pathway with capsaicin diet and idiopathic short
stature is interesting and may have translational potential. The exosome development is also of
potential interest.
Below are some concerns and suggestions.Major
Reviewer’s Comment: The origin of the chondrocytes used in the different experiments is not
clear. How were the human chondrocytes isolated?
Response： In our study, we identified significant overexpression of miR-17-3p in plasma
exosomes from patients with idiopathic short stature (ISS) and hypothesized that this
overexpression is a primary contributor to the short stature phenotype. To investigate the effects of
miR-17-3p on human growth plate chondrocytes, we utilized the C-28/I2 human chondrocyte cell
line (obtained from Otwo Biotech, Cat No. HTX2308), rather than primary chondrocytes. This
clarification has been included in lines 150 and 561 of the revised manuscript. This choice was
made due to ethical and practical constraints: obtaining growth plate chondrocytes from children
is not feasible due to ethical standards, and while chondrocytes could be isolated from articular
cartilage of adult patients undergoing joint replacement for severe arthritis, such cells are in a
pathological state and not representative of healthy growth plate chondrocytes. The C-28/I2 cell
line, derived from human juvenile costal cartilage, is widely recognized and extensively utilized in
cartilage biology, osteoarthritis research, and studies on cartilage repair. It is well-suited for
studying the effects of interfering factors, such as miR-17-3p, on chondrocyte proliferation,
differentiation, and ossification. We believe this cell line provides a reliable and reproducible
model for our in vitro experiments, and we have clarified its origin and rationale in the revised
manuscript.
Reviewer’s Comment: Hypertrophic chondrocytes typically don’t proliferate. Were different
culture timepoints used to examine proliferation and hypertrophic differentiation? More
experimental details would be useful and showing the chondrocyte phenotype through phase
contrast microscopy may be helpful.
Response： We fully agree with the reviewer’s point that hypertrophic chondrocytes typically do
not proliferate, and we have designed our experiments to distinguish between proliferation and
hypertrophic differentiation accordingly. To assess the impact of miR-17-3p on chondrocyte
proliferation, we overexpressed miR-17-3p in C-28/I2 chondrocytes using exosomes or adenovirus
for 72 hours, followed by analysis with the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay. CCK-8 is a
colorimetric assay that measures cell viability and proliferation based on the reduction of a
tetrazolium salt into a water-soluble formazan dye by dehydrogenase enzymes in metabolically
active cells, providing a quantitative readout of cell proliferation. In parallel, to evaluate
hypertrophic differentiation, we analyzed separate samples (also overexpressing miR-17-3p for 72
hours) using qPCR and Western blot (WB) to measure the expression of hypertrophic markers
RUNX2 and Collagen X, as commonly reported in the literature. These markers allowed us to
assess the effect of miR-17-3p on chondrocyte hypertrophic differentiation.
Regarding the chondrocyte phenotype, we acknowledge that in vitro cultured C-28/I2
chondrocytes adhere to the culture surface and exhibit a polygonal morphology, lacking the
pronounced hypertrophic phenotype observed in vivo in growth plate chondrocytes, as illustrated
in the figure below. Therefore, consistent with
approaches in the field, we relied on molecular
markers (e.g., RUNX2, Collagen X) rather
than phase contrast microscopy to evaluate
hypertrophic differentiation in vitro.
Additionally, to assess ossification, we
examined osteogenic markers (OCN and OPN)
using quantitative PCR (qPCR), Western blot
(WB), and staining techniques, including
Alizarin Red (for mineralization), Alkaline
Phosphatase (ALP) activity, and Von kossa
staining (for calcium deposition).
Recognizing the limitations of 2D in vitro culture in mimicking the 3D structure of the growth
plate, we complemented these experiments with ex vivo whole knee joint cultures. In these models,
miR-17-3p was overexpressed, and proliferation was assessed using BrdU incorporation.
Meanwhile, ossification and new bone growth rates were evaluated using Calcein staining.
Immunofluorescence further confirmed the expression of hypertrophic markers (RUNX2, Collagen
X) and osteogenic markers (OCN, OPN). Finally, we overexpressed miR-17-3p in mice and
analyzed its effects on growth plate chondrocyte proliferation, differentiation, and bone formation.
Reviewer’s Comment: In that previous study, only 13 differentially expressed miRNAs in the
ISS exosomes were found (vs 42 in the present study). Where do the authors attribute this
difference? What was the initial rationale for focusing on the miR-17-3p in the present study?
Were any other of the differentially identified miRNAs expressed in human chondrocytes?
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful questions regarding the differences in
the number of differentially expressed miRNAs between our previous study and the current work,
as well as the rationale for focusing on miR-17-3p. Below, we provide a detailed response to
address these points:
1. Difference in the Number of Differentially Expressed miRNAs:
In our previous study (PMID: 36927779), we identified 13 differentially expressed miRNAs in ISS
plasma exosomes using a 2-fold change threshold for significance. However, in the current study,
we applied a 1.5-fold change threshold, which resulted in the identification of 43 differentially
expressed miRNAs. This difference in the number of miRNAs is primarily attributed to the more
inclusive threshold used in the current analysis. Shanghai Biohao Biological Co., Ltd. provided
both the 1.5-fold and 2-fold threshold-based miRNA lists. We have included the complete raw data
(Excel file) containing the basic information of all differentially expressed miRNAs in the raw data
for transparency.
2. Rationale for Focusing on miR-17-3p:
The selection of miR-17-3p as the focus of the current study was based on a combination of
bioinformatics analysis, experimental validation, and its functional relevance to chondrocyte
biology. Below, we outline the key steps and rationale:
 Initial Findings and Hypothesis Development:
In our 2023 study, we reported that miR-26-3p was highly expressed in ISS plasma
exosomes and could inhibit chondrocyte proliferation and ossification, contributing to the
short-stature phenotype. However, the origin of this abnormal exosomal miRNA
expression remained unclear. To address this, we conducted a comprehensive literature
review and meta-analysis, combined with epidemiological data from China, which
revealed a higher incidence of ISS in regions with high capsaicin consumption. This led
us to hypothesize that capsaicin-induced intestinal inflammation might be a key factor
driving the abnormal expression of exosomal miRNAs in ISS patients.
 Experimental Validation in Animal Models:
To test this hypothesis, we conducted capsaicin diet experiments in rats. Through three
independent experiments, we consistently observed that capsaicin consumption induced a
short stature phenotype in rats. Subsequent analysis of plasma exosomes from these rats
revealed that miR-17-3p, rather than miR-26-3p, was significantly upregulated, closely
mimicking the elevated miR-17-3p levels observed in ISS patients. Additionally, we found
that LCN2 (lipocalin-2) was also highly expressed in the plasma of capsaicin-fed rats,
consistent with our 2022 report.
 Bioinformatics and Functional Screening:
After establishing the capsaicin-induced short stature model, we performed a
bioinformatics comparison of the 43 differentially expressed miRNAs identified in ISS
patients (with a 1.5-fold threshold) with their
rat homologs. Only 12 miRNAs showed 100%
sequence identity between rats and humans,
and among these, two miRNAs (miR-17-3p
and miR-1441-3p) were confirmed by qPCR
to be significantly differentially expressed in
chondrocytes.
Importantly, miR-17-3p exhibited the most
pronounced differential expression and, when
overexpressed in human chondrocytes,
demonstrated the most substantial inhibitory effects on proliferation and ossification,
outperforming miR-1441-3p. These findings led us to select miR-17-3p as the primary
candidate for further investigation.
Reviewer’s Comment: miR-17-3p appears to have similar effects on chondrocytes as the
previously published, exosome-derived, miR26b-3p. However, the authors don’t discuss this.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. In our previous study, we found that high
expression of plasma exosome-derived miR-26b-3p in ISS children inhibits chondrocyte
proliferation and cartilage ossification, resulting in a short stature phenotype in experimental
animals. However, the reason for the elevated miR-26b-3p levels in plasma exosomes and its
organ of origin remains unclear. Building on the observation of a higher incidence of ISS in
regions with high capsaicin diets in China, we established a capsaicin diet animal model. In this
model, rats exhibited a short stature phenotype, with normal expression of growth hormone and
insulin-like growth factor, mimicking the pathological features of ISS (i.e., intact hypothalamic
growth hormone and IGF axis function).
More importantly, in the capsaicin diet rats, plasma exosome miR-17-3p was significantly
upregulated compared to the control group (p < 0.001), recapitulating the plasma exosome
miR-17-3p expression profile observed in ISS patients. While we also observed higher plasma
exosome miR-26b-3p expression in the capsaicin diet group compared to the control group, this
difference did not reach statistical significance. Consequently, we did not discuss the role of
miR-26b-3p in the context of the capsaicin diet in the current manuscript.
Although the capsaicin diet rat model did not replicate the statistically significant
upregulation of miR-26b-3p, we identified elevated expression of the LCN2 protein in the plasma
of these rats, consistent with our previous findings reported in 2022 (Liu X, Zhang J, Yuan J, Ding
R, Liu T, Jia J. LCN2 is a new diagnostic biomarker and potential therapeutic target in idiopathic
short stature. J Cell Mol Med. 2022;26(12):3568-3581). Additionally, we observed increased
TNXB protein expression in the plasma of capsaicin-fed rats, a finding also mirrored in the
plasma of ISS patients. However, the specific mechanisms underlying TNXB upregulation remain
unclear and are currently under investigation.
The lack of statistical significance in miR-26b-3p expression in the capsaicin diet rats could
be attributed to the limited sample size or potential differences in genetic backgrounds between
humans and rats, which may prevent identical pathological manifestations. Nevertheless, it is
noteworthy that our capsaicin diet model not only successfully induced a short-stature phenotype
but also demonstrated consistent changes in multiple molecular markers (e.g., miR-17-3p, LCN2,
and TNXB) that align with observations in ISS patients. Furthermore, similar trends were detected
in fecal samples from ISS patients, reinforcing the relevance of this model. These findings suggest
that the capsaicin diet animal model holds significant value for studying the pathogenesis of ISS in
regions with high capsaicin consumption.
Reviewer’s Comment: Please include in the methods details on the ex vivo growth plate cartilage
experiments. How was the miRNA overexpressed and how were the different genes knocked out?
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestion. We have addressed your request by
incorporating detailed information about the ex vivo growth plate cartilage experiments into the
Materials and Methods section (Lines 706–731) of the revised manuscript. Specifically, we have
clarified the methodology for miR-17-3p overexpression and the CRISPR-Cas9-mediated
knockdown of ZNF148 and SOS1 in fetal SD rat femur explant cultures. These additions outline
the lentiviral transfection process, culture conditions, and analytical techniques employed. We
believe these revisions enhance the transparency of our experimental approach and fully address
your comment. Please let us know if further clarification is needed.
Revised Added Content:
Explant Culture of Fetal SD Rat Femurs with miR-17-3p Overexpression and ZNF148/SOS1
Knockdown
Approval for the use of rat limbs was granted by the Animal Ethics Committee of Nanchang
University. Femurs from fetal Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats were harvested one day postpartum. The
explanted tissues were statically cultured in BGJb medium (Gibco, Australia) supplemented with 6
mg/ml bovine serum albumin (BSA; Gibco, Australia), 150 µg/ml ascorbic acid (Solarbio, Cat:
A8100), 100 units/ml penicillin, and 100 µg/ml streptomycin (Gibco, Australia). Cultures were
maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2, with the medium refreshed daily
using freshly prepared reagents.
For gene editing and overexpression, CRISPR-Cas9 knockdown plasmids targeting ZNF148
and SOS1, along with an miR-17-3p overexpression plasmid, were obtained from Guangzhou
VectorBuilder Co., Ltd. and Genechem Co., Ltd. (China). Detailed plasmid sequences are
provided in Supplementary Fig. 24c–f. Lentiviral particles were generated by transfecting
HEK293T cells with the corresponding lentiviral packaging plasmids. The resulting supernatants
were collected, filtered, and concentrated using a Virus Concentration Kit (Beyotime, Cat:
C2901S) to achieve a titer exceeding 1×10^8 TU/ml (quantified by p24 ELISA). Concentrated
lentiviral stocks were stored at -80°C in PBS with 1% BSA.
Transfection of fetal rat growth plate cartilage was performed in a 2 ml culture system using
a 24-well plate. Concentrated lentiviral supernatant (titer > 5×10^8 FU/ml, multiplicity of
infection [MOI] = 200) was mixed with 8 µg/ml polybrene and HiTransG A (Genechem Co., Ltd.,
Shanghai), a specialized transfection reagent, to enhance transduction efficiency. The explants
were transduced with lentiviral particles carrying either the ZNF148/SOS1 knockdown constructs
or the miR-17-3p overexpression construct in fresh medium. The medium was replaced 72 hours
post-transfection and refreshed daily thereafter. After 14 days of culture, samples were analyzed by
RT-qPCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence. Experimental groupings are detailed in
Supplementary Fig. 27.
Reviewer’s Comment: The authors hypothesize that the capsaicin diet is a crucial causative
factor (through the demonstrated miR-17-3p pathway) for ISS. Is a diet history available for the
individuals with ISS vs the control group?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this insightful question about the availability of
dietary history data for individuals with ISS and the control group. Below, we provide a detailed
response:
In this retrospective study, we did not collect detailed dietary histories, including capsaicin
consumption, from the ISS patients or controls. This limitation stems from the challenges of
obtaining accurate and reliable dietary records in a retrospective design. Nevertheless, our
hypothesis that capsaicin consumption contributes to ISS via the miR-17-3p pathway is supported
by multiple lines of indirect evidence, as outlined below.
Epidemiological Evidence:
We observed a higher incidence of ISS in regions of China where capsaicin-rich diets are
prevalent, suggesting a potential association between dietary capsaicin and ISS.
Animal Model Evidence:
In our capsaicin diet-induced rat model, we successfully recapitulated key ISS features, including
elevated plasma exosomal miR-17-3p levels and a short stature phenotype. These findings
reinforce the role of capsaicin in the pathogenesis of ISS.
Human Intervention Study:
To explore the causal link between capsaicin consumption and miR-17-3p upregulation, we
conducted a preliminary intervention study with eight adult volunteers (children were excluded
due to ethical concerns regarding repeated blood sampling and the pilot nature of the experiment).
Participants followed a 4-week protocol with alternating periods of no capsaicin diet, capsaicin
diet, and no capsaicin diet, during which blood and fecal samples were collected. Key findings
include:
 Capsaicin Diet Phase: Plasma exosomal miR-17-3p levels significantly increased and
correlated positively with intestinal inflammation markers.
 Post-Capsaicin Phase: miR-17-3p levels declined after cessation of the capsaicin diet.
 Reintroduction Phase: miR-17-3p levels increased again upon resumption of the
capsaicin diet.
These results provide preliminary direct evidence of a causal relationship between
capsaicin intake and the upregulation of miR-17-3p.
To directly investigate the link between capsaicin consumption and ISS, we are planning a
prospective, multicenter study. This will include comprehensive dietary assessments (e.g., food
frequency questionnaires or dietary logs) for both ISS patients and controls. Such data will enable
a more robust evaluation of our hypothesis that high capsaicin intake contributes to ISS via the
miR-17-3p pathway.

shown in Group D. When miR-17-3p was overexpressed, administering growth hormone (GH)
alone failed to restore the rats’ height to normal levels, indicating that miR-17-3p not only induces

exosomes carrying both si-miR-17-3p and GH), which outperformed Group C (non-targeted
exosomes carrying si-miR-17-3p and GH). These findings indicate that while exosomes carrying
both siRNA and GH are effective for ISS treatment, cartilage-targeted exosomes provide superior
therapeutic outcomes compared to non-targeted exosomes, demonstrating enhanced efficacy in
promoting height recovery and highlighting their potential for clinical applications.

the growth plate. Did these exosomes also localize to other tissues, such as articular cartilage,
the brain, or blood vessels? Why did they localize to the skull?

mechanism of collagen type II-coated exosomes to the growth plate, as well as their potential
localization to other tissues such as articular cartilage, the brain, or blood vessels, and the
observed localization to the skull. We greatly appreciate your inquiry, which has encouraged us to
provide a more detailed explanation to improve the manuscript’s clarity.
In our study, we employed a membrane fusion protein technique to load the exosome surface
with the collagen type II-targeting peptide WYRGRL. This modification confers specificity to
tissues rich in collagen type II, such as the growth plate cartilage and articular cartilage,
enabling the targeted delivery of exosomes (Lines 668-675). Tissues like the brain and blood
vessels, which contain negligible amounts of collagen type II, showed no significant targeting, as
expected due to the peptide’s selective affinity. Regarding the skull localization observed in our in
vivo imaging, we used 4- to 6-week-old rats for these experiments—a developmental stage during
which the skull undergoes endochondral ossification to complete bony fusion. Since this process
involves collagen type II-rich cartilage, the fluorescence signal detected in the skull reflects the
targeting of our exosomes to this transient cartilaginous tissue.
We have incorporated these details into the revised manuscript, and the Materials and
Methods section now includes a detailed description of the experimental procedures and targeting
specificity (Lines 668-675).

Reviewer’s Comment: In line 213 the authors indicate that the exosomes were produced by
chondrocytes, but I had the impression that they were produced by the gut villi- please explain
what is the origin of the exosomes? what do you think was the origin of the exosomes in the
children?
Response: We thank the reviewer for their insightful comment. Below, we clarify the origin of
exosomes referenced in line 213 and provide our hypothesis regarding the origin of exosomes in
ISS children, as well as the rationale for our experimental design.
Clarification on Exosomes in Line 213 (Chondrocyte-Derived Exosomes):
In our study, we initially observed that plasma exosomes from ISS children inhibited the
proliferation of human chondrocytes (C28 cell line) and suppressed the expression of
chondrogenic differentiation markers. Through high-throughput sequencing and qPCR validation,
we identified miR-17-3p as highly expressed in these exosomes. To further investigate the role of
miR-17-3p, we used chondrocyte-derived exosomes overexpressing miR-17-3p for both in vitro
and in vivo experiments.
We chose chondrocyte-derived exosomes for the following reasons:
 At the time of these experiments, the cellular origin of the abnormally expressed exosomes
in ISS children’s plasma was unknown.
 Using chondrocyte-derived exosomes allowed us to specifically overexpress miR-17-3p
while maintaining other exosomal contents derived from chondrocytes. This approach
helped us isolate the effects of miR-17-3p overexpression on chondrocyte proliferation
and bone formation, without confounding factors from other cell types.
These experiments demonstrated that miR-17-3p inhibits growth plate chondrocyte proliferation
and bone formation in vivo, leading to a short-stature phenotype.
Hypothesized Origin of Exosomes in ISS Children (Gut-Derived):
In subsequent experiments, we investigated the potential source of the exosomes in ISS children.
Using a capsaicin-induced mouse model, we observed a short-stature phenotype. However, we
found no difference in blood capsaicin levels between the capsaicin diet group and the control
group, suggesting that capsaicin does not directly enter the bloodstream to inhibit growth plate
chondrogenesis.
Further analysis of intestinal tissues revealed inflammatory cell infiltration and activation of
the NF-κB signaling pathway, accompanied by upregulated miR-17-3p expression. In vitro
experiments confirmed that capsaicin activates NF-κB and induces miR-17-3p overexpression.
Additionally, we detected elevated levels of miR-17-3p and inflammatory markers (IL-1β and
TNF-α) in the feces of ISS children.
Based on these findings, we propose that the abnormally expressed exosomes in the plasma
of ISS children originate from the intestinal tract, likely due to chronic intestinal inflammation and
NF-κB-mediated upregulation of miR-17-3p.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Idiopathic short stature (ISS) remains a major pediatric challenge with unclear causes and inconsistent responses to growth hormone therapy. Here we show that plasma exosomes from children with ISS contain elevated hsa-miR-17-3p that disrupts growth signaling and impairs cartilage cell proliferation. Elevated miR-17-3p suppresses ZNF148/SOS1 signaling, linking molecular dysfunction to dietary exposure in ISS. To investigate environmental triggers, we developed a capsaicin-rich diet rat model that recapitulates ISS, showing normal Gh/Igf-1 levels but elevated plasma miR-17-3p. The diet induced mild gut inflammation, increasing miR-17-3p in intestinal and plasma exosomes. Fecal samples from ISS children exhibited similar elevations in miR-17-3p and inflammatory markers, linking spicy diets to ISS pathogenesis. Finally, engineered exosomes designed to silence miR-17-3p, combined with localized growth hormone therapy, restored growth plate function. These findings uncover a diet-driven exosome axis underlying ISS and suggest new therapeutic strategies for children in high-capsaicin regions.

---

## Introduction

Short stature is defined as a child’s height being less than two standard deviations or below the 3rd percentile of the average human height of children of the same sex, age, and race1–3. This condition may have significant implications for the physical and psychological well-being of affected children. Previous research studies have shown that anxiety scores and depression scores are significantly higher in children with short stature than in the control group4. As a result, these challenges often persist into adulthood. Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) offers hope for treating children with short stature, especially in cases of growth hormone deficiency5. However, the majority of cases are ultimately classified as idiopathic short stature (ISS) after ruling out systemic diseases, nutritional deficiencies, psychiatric disorders, chromosomal abnormalities, and growth hormone deficiency, yet their cause remains unknown1,6,7. ISS represents 30–80% of short-stature cases1,6, but its underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. Unlike children with growth hormone deficiency-related short stature, those with ISS have normal growth hormone levels7. During clinical treatment, it is not uncommon for ISS children to show insensitivity to rhGH therapy. As a result, rhGH treatment for ISS requires higher dosages and shows varying levels of effectiveness compared to treatments for the short stature of growth hormone deficiency. The efficacy and safety of rhGH therapy continue to be topics of debate.

Hou et al.8 reported an average height gain of 9.55 ± 0.13 cm after one year of rhGH treatment in 200 Chinese children with ISS (average age 9.03 ± 0.21 years; 68.5% boys, 31.5% girls), whereas Yoo et al. noted an increase of 10.68 ± 1.95 cm9. In contrast, research by Van et al.10 and Kamp et al.11 reported that while rhGH therapy may enhance height during treatment, it could accelerate growth plate closure, resulting in adult heights that do not significantly differ from those of untreated controls. These findings highlight the variable efficacy of rhGH therapy in achieving long-term height improvement.

In terms of safety, while some studies have raised concerns about potential risks associated with rhGH therapy, such as bone and cartilage tumors, cerebrovascular diseases, hypertension, insulin resistance, and brain hemorrhages12–14, other large-scale studies, including those by Savendahl et al. and Cianfarani et al., indicate that rhGH treatment is generally safe when used appropriately, particularly in low-risk patients15,16. Nevertheless, the long-term safety profile of rhGH therapy, especially regarding specific risks, remains an area of ongoing research and surveillance.

The 2016 American Academy of Pediatric Endocrinology guidelines emphasize that rhGH therapy is not universally recommended for all ISS patients, particularly those with less severe short stature (height standard deviation score [HtSDS] above −2.25) or those without significant physical or psychosocial burdens related to their condition17. This underscores the limitation of rhGH therapy in ISS, including its variable efficacy and potential risks. Additionally, the high cost of rhGH treatment, estimated at $10 billion annually in the United States18, further limits accessibility and highlights the need for alternative therapies. Given these challenges, a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ISS is crucial for developing more effective and targeted treatments.

In recent years, researchers have pinpointed specific ISS susceptibility genes using whole-genome sequencing. These genes include GHR, SHOX, FGFR3, ACAN, and NPR219–23. However, the mutation rate of these genes is only 1–5%, which significantly limits their potential application in clinical treatment despite being beneficial for further ISS typing. Additionally, while the hypothalamic-GH-IGF axis is a crucial pathway regulating childhood linear growth, most ISS patients do not exhibit significant abnormalities in this area.

As the terminal regulatory organ of the hypothalamic-GH-IGF axis, the growth plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth through endochondral ossification. It determines final adult height, serving as the “engine” of height development. Analyzing the molecular pathological changes in the growth plates of ISS children could elucidate their pathogenesis. However, the ethical challenges of obtaining growth plate samples from ISS children presents significant barriers to etiological research and the development of new treatments.

It is well known that various hormones and growth factors secreted by tissues and organs are delivered to the growth plate via the bloodstream, interacting with it to regulate growth and development through intercellular signaling processes. Previous studies have indicated no abnormalities in the secretion of growth hormone, glucocorticoids, and thyroid hormones in the circulation of ISS patients. However, blood circulation contains numerous exosomes besides hormones and growth factors.

Exosomes, small lipid-bilayer vesicles, play a critical role in cell communication and pathology by transporting proteins, miRNAs, and other molecules between cells24–26. Natural nanoparticles have significant potential for drug delivery since they can cross biological barriers without causing immunogenic reactions27. Although exosomes show potential for advancing our understanding and treatment of ISS, their specific role in the pathogenesis of ISS remains largely unclear and warrants further investigation.

Our study demonstrates that plasma-derived exosomes from ISS children markedly inhibit chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation, an effect linked to hsa-miR-17-3p overexpression. However, the origin of elevated plasma exosomal miR-17-3p in ISS remains unclear. To investigate this, we reviewed epidemiological data and found that ISS prevalence is higher in Chinese regions with high capsaicin consumption—such as Jiangxi, Chongqing, Hunan, and Guizhou—collectively home to over 200 million people28. Zou et al.29 reported that Hunan Province has the highest total annual pepper consumption (7.57 million tons), followed by Jiangxi, Guizhou, Chongqing, Yunnan, and Hubei. The combined population of these six provinces is approximately 286.8 million. Based on per capita pepper consumption, the upper and middle reaches of the Yangtze River were classified as “extreme-spicy” areas, including Hunan (111.57 kg/person/year), Guizhou (98.5 kg), Jiangxi (97.6 kg), and Chongqing (95.6 kg).

These large-scale observations suggest a potential link between habitual high-capsaicin intake and ISS pathogenesis, with significant public health implications. The capsaicin dietary model used in our animal experiments was developed to reflect the epidemiological characteristics of these high-incidence regions, where capsaicin-rich diets are a common part of daily life.

In subsequent experiments, a capsaicin-enriched diet—designed as a model to simulate the chili consumption levels observed in these high-prevalence areas—induced mild intestinal inflammation in Sprague-Dawley rats. This inflammation activated the NF-κB signaling pathway, identified as the main driver of elevated plasma exosomal miR-17-3p levels. To our knowledge, this is the first study to directly connect dietary capsaicin, gut inflammation, and ISS pathogenesis, providing new insight into ISS etiology.

Furthermore, we engineered exosomes with growth plate-targeting capabilities to deliver siRNA, effectively counteracting the inhibitory effects of miR-17-3p overexpression while allowing precise local growth hormone administration. This approach significantly enhanced therapeutic outcomes for short stature, representing a promising and innovative treatment strategy. The findings of this study not only deepen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying ISS but also propose a groundbreaking avenue for targeted therapeutic interventions with the potential to revolutionize current treatment approaches. Finally, our results emphasize the necessity of increasing attention to the impact of capsaicin-rich diets on children’s longitudinal growth, particularly among high-risk ISS populations and short-statured children receiving growth hormone therapy.

## Results

Characterization of plasma exosomes
Plasma exosomes from ISS patients and healthy controls were isolated via ultracentrifugation and characterized using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and Western blotting. TEM revealed cup-shaped or spherical exosomes, with Nano-Sight analysis indicating a predominant diameter of 100 nm (Fig. 1a, b). Western blotting confirmed the presence of exosomal markers CD81, CD9, and CD63 in both ISS and control samples (Fig. 1c). Successful uptake of FAM-labeled exosomes (indicated by green fluorescence) by human chondrocytes C28/I2 (blue fluorescence) was verified (Fig. 1e).

Impaired chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation induced by plasma exosomes from ISS children
Human chondrocytes co-cultured with plasma exosomes from ISS children exhibited a marked reduction in proliferation, as shown by EdU and CCK-8 assays (Fig. 1d, f, g). Flow cytometric analysis indicated an increased proportion of cells in the G0/G1 phase and a corresponding decrease in the S phases in the ISS-Exos group compared to controls (Fig. 1h, i). RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses revealed significant downregulation of chondrocyte hypertrophic differentiation markers (COL10A1, RUNX2) and osteogenic marker genes (OPN, OCN). Moreover, ALP activity was markedly reduced, and positive staining for Von Kossa and Alizarin Red decreased in the ISS-Exos group (Fig. 1j, k, l, m). These results suggest that plasma exosomes from ISS children impair chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation.

Identification of miR-17-3p as a diagnostic biomarker in ISS via high-throughput sequencing of plasma exosomal miRNAs
High-throughput sequencing of plasma exosomal miRNAs identified 42 differentially expressed miRNAs, including 31 upregulated and 11 downregulated (Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). RT-qPCR analysis demonstrated a significant upregulation of miR-17-3p in the plasma exosomes of ISS children (Supplementary Fig. 1c). An area under the curve (AUC) of 0.976 (95% CI, 0.959–0.993) was observed for miR-17-3p, with an optimal cutoff point of >1.2955, yielding a specificity of 89.62% and sensitivity of 98.13% for distinguishing children with ISS from healthy controls. (Supplementary Fig. 1d). In situ hybridization analysis demonstrated that miR-17-3p is expressed in human chondrocytes (C28 cell line) and is also localized in the growth plate cartilage of SD rats. In situ hybridization revealed localization of miR-17-3p expression in human chondrocytes versus SD rat growth plate region (Supplementary Fig. 1e). GO and KEGG pathway analyses indicated that genes targeted by the overexpression of miR-17-3p are enriched in the PI3K-Akt, RAS, and MEK signaling pathways (Supplementary Fig. 1f, g).

miR-17-3p as the key mediator of ISS Exosome-Induced inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation
Exosomes from ISS children inhibited chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation, which was reversed by downregulating miR-17-3p expression in ISS exosomes (Fig. 2a–j). Furthermore, the overexpression of miR-17-3p in human chondrocytes significantly suppresses proliferation, as demonstrated by CCK-8, cell cycle, and EdU assays (Supplementary Fig. 2a–f). Hypertrophic differentiation markers (COL10A1, RUNX2) and osteogenic markers genes (OPN, OCN) were also downregulated, and osteoblastic activity, indicated by ALP staining, and bone formation capacity, evidenced by Von Kossa and Alizarin Red staining, were significantly reduced (Supplementary Fig. 2g-j). This indicates that ISS exosomes inhibit chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation by overexpressing miR-17-3p.

Given that two-dimensional chondrocyte cultures do not fully replicate the biological effects of miR-17-3p overexpression in growth plate cartilage, we performed whole-knee joint organ cultures of neonatal rats. The results mirrored those observed in chondrocyte cultures. Overall bone growth and development were impaired, with reduced expression of hypertrophic differentiation marker genes (COL10A1, RUNX2) and osteogenic marker genes (OCN, OPN) (Supplementary Fig. 3a-i).

miR-17-3p Targets the ZNF148/SOS1 axis to regulate chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation
High-throughput mRNA sequencing following miR-17-3p overexpression identified 77 upregulated and 166 downregulated genes with differential expression (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Western blotting and RT-qPCR validated decreased ZNF148 expression in human chondrocytes after overexpressing miR-17-3p (Supplementary Fig. 4c and Fig. 5b–d). Dual luciferase assays confirmed direct interaction, with reduced luciferase activity following co-transfection with wild-type miR-17-3p/ZNF148 mimics (Supplementary Fig. 4f, g). Rescue experiments with ZNF148 overexpression countered the inhibitory effects of miR-17-3p on proliferation and bone formation (Supplementary Fig. 5a–m).

Bioinformatics analysis identified SOS1 (Son of Sevenless homolog 1) as a downstream target regulated by ZNF148 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses demonstrated the downregulation of ZNF148 and SOS1 following miR-17-3p overexpression (Supplementary Fig. 6a–d). Rescue experiments with SOS1 overexpression reversed the inhibitory effects of miR-17-3p on chondrocyte proliferation and ossification, as evidenced by EdU, CCK-8 assays, cell cycle analysis, and molecular marker evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 6). ChIP-seq and agarose gel electrophoresis validated ZNF148’s binding to the SOS1 (Supplementary Fig. 7b–d). A significant reduction in SOS1 expression at both mRNA and protein levels was also detected by knockdown of ZNF148 (Supplementary Fig. 7e–g). These findings suggest that miR-17-3p regulates chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation through the ZNF148/SOS1 axis.

The Role of ZNF148 and SOS1 in regulating chondrocyte proliferation and growth plate development
Using CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out ZNF148 or SOS1 in human chondrocytes and neonatal rat growth plate cartilage, we investigated their roles in chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation. The knockout of ZNF148 or SOS1 significantly impaired chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation (Supplementary Figs. 8, 9). Rescue experiments in which SOS1 was overexpressed in ZNF148-deficient chondrocytes restored proliferation and endochondral ossification/bone formation (Supplementary Fig. 10). Ex vivo cultures of neonatal rat knee joints confirmed these findings, showing reduced chondrocyte proliferation and downregulated differentiation markers (COL10A1, RUNX2) and osteogenic markers genes (OCN, OPN) in ZNF148 or SOS1 knockout groups (Supplementary Figs. 11, 12).

miR-17-3p targets the ZNF148/SOS1 axis and modulates MEK and PI3K pathways to regulate chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation
Enrichment analysis of differentially expressed mRNAs following miR-17-3p overexpression identified significant enrichment in the MEK and PI3K pathways, highlighting their role in miR-17-3p-mediated suppression of chondrocyte proliferation and endochondral ossification/bone formation (Supplementary Fig. 4d, e). RT-qPCR and Western blot analyses revealed that SOS1 knockout did not alter the mRNA or protein expression levels of key MEK and PI3K pathway genes, including ERK1/2, PI3K, and AKT. However, SOS1 knockout significantly decreased RAS expression and the phosphorylation levels of ERK1/2, PI3K, and AKT (Supplementary Fig. 9a–e and Fig. 12g, j, k). This in vitro experiment indicates that SOS1 exerts its biological effects by regulating the phosphorylation of these proteins, thereby inhibiting the RAS/ERK and PI3K pathways. This finding was further validated by in vivo experiments in rats (Figs. 3, 4 and Supplementary Fig. 18).

Exosomal miR-17-3p inhibits growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation in vivo, leading to a short-stature phenotype
In vivo studies demonstrated that overexpression of miR-17-3p, using exosomes derived from primary rat chondrocytes isolated from the proximal tibia and distal femur growth plates, induced a short-stature phenotype in immature rats (Figs. 3–4). RT-qPCR confirmed overexpression of miR-17-3p in plasma and growth plate cartilage (Supplementary Fig. 24b). Safranin O and Fast Green staining, Calcein labeling, RT-qPCR, and Western blot analyses showed decreased overall growth plate thickness with a reduced rate of new bone formation, decreased expression of hypertrophic differentiation marker genes (Col10a1, Runx2) and osteogenic marker genes (Ocn, Opn) (Fig. 3a–p).

Capsaicin-induced short-stature phenotype and elevated plasma miR-17-3p expression in immature rats
Although we are the first to report elevated miR-17-3p levels in plasma-derived exosomes from children with ISS, the underlying causes and sources of this overexpression of miR-17-3p remain unclear. Epidemiological data reveal that the incidence of ISS is significantly higher in Chongqing, Jiangxi, Sichuan, Guizhou, Hunan provinces, and Chongqing municipalities in China, regions where high chili pepper consumption is a prevalent dietary habit28,30,31. In response, we developed an ISS animal model by administering a capsaicin-enriched diet to immature rats. Analysis of the capsaicin (0.01% supplemented) and control (capsaicin-free) diet groups revealed that during the first four days, the average daily food intake in the capsaicin group was slightly lower than that in the control group (Supplementary Fig. 25a). This reduced intake in the capsaicin group during the initial four days is likely attributable to a short-term adaptation to the transition from a capsaicin-free to a capsaicin-supplemented diet. From day six onward, the daily food intake of the capsaicin group showed no statistically significant difference compared to the control group, indicating adequate palatability of the capsaicin diet (Supplementary Fig. 25a). However, by the end of the 28-day experiment, the capsaicin group exhibited significantly lower body weight and height compared to the control group (Supplementary Fig. 25b, c). The weight-to-length ratio (WLR), calculated as WLR = weight (g) ÷ length (cm), was 6.29 g/cm for the capsaicin group and 6.03 g/cm for the control group, with no statistically significant difference between the groups. These findings suggest that the reduced stature in the capsaicin group resulted from the 0.01% capsaicin diet inhibiting growth and development, rather than reduced food intake due to poor diet palatability. Remarkably, capsaicin-diet not only suppressed growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation, thereby successfully inducing a short-stature phenotype (Fig. 5), but also elevated miR-17-3p levels in the plasma of these rats (Supplementary Fig. 24a). This finding aligns with the elevated plasma miR-17-3p observed in ISS children, providing further insight into the potential link between the capsaicin diet and miR-17-3p expression in ISS.

We further performed a comprehensive histological examination of the intestinal tissues to elucidate the mechanism behind the elevated miR-17-3p expression observed in capsaicin-fed rats. This analysis uncovered significant structural disruptions in the villi, along with marked infiltration of inflammatory cells in the small intestines and colon of the capsaicin-treated group (Supplementary Fig. 14a, b and Supplementary Fig. 16). Elevated activities of myeloperoxidase (MPO) and malondialdehyde (MDA) provided evidence of oxidative stress and a likely inflammatory response (Supplementary Fig. 14c, d). ELISA assays revealed a notable increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines Il-1β, Il-10 and Tnf-α in the capsaicin-exposed rats (Supplementary Fig. 14e–g).

Previous research identified 84 differentially expressed plasma proteins in children with ISS, with 42 of these proteins associated with inflammatory pathways. Bioinformatic analysis indicated that 43% of these inflammatory proteins are regulated by the transcription factor NF-κB, implicating its involvement in the inflammatory response observed in ISS (Supplementary Fig. 13). The P65 subunit of the NF-κB protein complex regulates up to 50% of inflammation-related proteins in children with ISS (Supplementary Fig. 13). Subsequent Western blot and RT-qPCR analyses corroborated these findings, revealing elevated expression of phosphorylated p65 and Iκb in the intestinal tissues of capsaicin-fed rats, indicative of intensified NF-κB signaling (Supplementary Fig. 14l, o, and p). This was accompanied by a concurrent increase in miR-17-3p expression in the small intestine (Supplementary Fig. 14h).

To further explore the role of capsaicin in triggering intestinal inflammation and to elucidate the regulatory interplay between NF-κB and miR-17-3p, we conducted in vitro studies using the small intestinal epithelial cell line HIEC-6 and the healthy colon mucosal epithelial cell line NCM460 subjected to capsaicin stimulation. At lower concentrations, capsaicin promoted cellular proliferation, while higher concentrations, particularly at 200 µM, significantly inhibited cell growth and induced substantial apoptosis (Supplementary Fig. 15a–d and Supplementary Fig. 17a–f). This optimal concentration induced significant apoptosis (Supplementary Fig. 15e, f and Supplementary Fig. 17g–i) and elevated expression levels of both miR-17-3p and NF-κB (Supplementary Fig. 15h–k and Supplementary Fig. 17j-n). Notably, applying the NF-κB inhibitor bortezomib reduced miR-17-3p expression, underscoring that capsaicin activates NF-κB, subsequently driving the upregulation of miR-17-3p (Supplementary Fig. 15g–k and Supplementary Fig. 17j–n).

Elevated miR-17-3p in Stool Samples of ISS Children
To investigate the presence of gut inflammation and the expression of miR-17-3p in children’s ISS, we performed RT-qPCR or ELISA analyses on stool samples collected from both ISS patients and healthy controls. The results revealed a pronounced elevation in miR-17-3p and TNF-α levels in ISS children compared to their healthy counterparts, suggesting that the heightened miR-17-3p expression in ISS may be a consequence of underlying intestinal inflammation (Supplementary Fig. 14m, n).

ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH Antagonizes miR-17-3p-Induced Inhibition of Chondrocyte Proliferation and Bone Formation in Human Chondrocyte and Restores Height in Rats
To effectively target and eliminate aberrant miR-17-3p expression in growth plate cartilage and enable precise delivery of growth hormone (GH) for ISS treatment, we utilized membrane fusion protein technology to engineer exosomes displaying type II collagen peptides on their surface, enhancing their specificity for growth plate cartilage. These exosomes were subsequently loaded with miR-17-3p siRNA and GH. The resulting engineered exosomes, specifically designed for this purpose, are referred to as ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH.

Transmission electron microscopy confirmed the morphology of the exosomes, revealing a characteristic spherical or cup-shaped structure (Fig. 6a). Nano-Sight analysis indicated that the exosomes have an average diameter of approximately 150 nm (Fig. 6b). Zeta potential measurements using Zetaview (Particle Metrix) showed a negative surface charge of about -50 mV (Fig. 6c). Western blotting confirmed the presence of the exosomal markers CD81, CD9 and CD63 (Fig. 6d). The efficiency of GH loading into ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH was demonstrated by a dose-dependent increase in GH content, with 200 μg of ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH encapsulating nearly 100 ng of GH (Fig. 6e, g). Additionally, RT-qPCR confirmed the presence of siRNA-miR-17-3p within ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH (Fig. 6f, h). Co-culturing human chondrocytes with ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH demonstrated robust exosome uptake, GH internalization, and siRNA overexpression (Fig. 6i, j).

Frozen tissue sections corroborated the effective delivery of siRNA-miR-17-3p and GH protein by ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH to the growth plate cartilage (Fig. 6l). In vivo bioluminescence imaging assessed cartilage targeting, revealing a significantly higher accumulation of ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH in the growth plates of extremities compared to NC-Exos over time. Conversely, markedly fewer exosomes were detected in the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, and pancreas (Fig. 6k and Supplementary Fig. 22), underscoring the specificity of ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH for targeting growth plate cartilage. Preliminary data from histological and biochemical analyses suggest that Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH exhibits no significant toxicity in major organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys (Supplementary Fig. 23). However, further studies are needed to confirm its comprehensive biosafety profile.

Subsequent in vitro experiments showed that ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH attenuated miR-17-3p overexpression inhibitory effects on chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation, as illustrated in Fig. 7. Following overexpression of miR-17-3p in neonatal rats, Safranin O and Fast Green staining revealed a decrease in overall growth plate thickness (Fig. 8i), and calcein labeling further highlighted a significant reduction in new bone formation (Fig. 8g, h), as well as a reduction in the expression of markers of hypertrophic differentiation (Col10a1 and Runx2) and osteogenic genes (Ocn and Opn) (Fig. 8j, k). Consequently, the rats displayed a short stature phenotype (Fig. 8a–f). Despite administering growth hormone therapy, height did not normalize compared to the control group, reflecting insensitivity to growth hormone therapy similar to that observed in clinical cases of ISS. In contrast, treatment with ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH demonstrated exceptional therapeutic efficacy in addressing the short stature induced by miR-17-3p overexpression, as shown in both in vitro and in vivo experiments (Figs. 7, 8). RT-qPCR demonstrated the levels of miR-17-3p in each group (Supplementary Fig. 24c, d).

Engineered Growth Plate Cartilage-Targeted Exosomes derived from Bone Marrow Mesenchymal Stem Cells similarly counteract miR-17-3p-induced inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and bone formation in human chondrocytes and restore height in rats
Compared to chondrocyte-derived exosomes, mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes are more readily obtainable and hold incredible promise for clinical applications. Therefore, we evaluated the efficacy of engineered growth plate-targeted exosomes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells in treating short stature. In the present study, we established a stable line of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells capable of secreting exosomes with consistent properties. Morphological characterization confirmed the exosomes’ spherical or cup-shaped structure (Supplementary Fig. 19a), with an average particle size of approximately 150 nm (Supplementary Fig. 19b) and a negative zeta potential (Supplementary Fig. 19c), Western blotting confirmed the presence of the exosomal markers CD81, CD9 and CD63 (Supplementary Fig. 19d). In vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrated the targeted delivery capabilities of the engineered exosomes and load capacity and confirmed their effectiveness in treating short stature (Supplementary Figs. 19–21). RT-qPCR demonstrated the levels of miR-17-3p in each group (Supplementary Fig. 24e, f).
