## Methods

Clinical Sample Characteristics and Plasma Exosome Collection
These 106 ISS patients and 106 age- and gender-matched controls were recruited from the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University, China. The ISS group comprised 52 males and 54 females (median age: 9.3 years, IQR: 7.475–10.50; median height: 125.6 cm, IQR: 116.3–133). The control group included 57 males and 49 females (median age: 9.55 years, IQR: 7.7–10.8; median height: 137.5 cm, IQR: 129.7–144.7) (Supplementary Table 1). Exclusion criteria encompassed: (i) skeletal anomalies or dysmorphic features at birth, (ii) hormonal abnormalities such as growth hormone (GH) deficiency (peak level <6 ng/mL) or thyroid and pubertal disorders, (iii) environmental or chronic conditions impacting growth, (iv) chromosomal aberrations detected cytogenetically, and (v) whole-exome sequencing findings.

Whole blood samples were collected between October 2016 and March 2023, and plasma was used to isolate exosomes according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Exosome Isolation and Purification Kit, Umibio, Cat No. UR52151). Exosome samples were stored at -80°C. Five pairs of samples underwent miRNA High-Throughput Sequencing for miRNA expression analysis, while all 212 samples were used for quantitative RT-PCR validation. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of the Second Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University (Approval No. [2024](50)). Written informed consent was obtained from participants’ guardians if under 14 years of age.

We collected 5 ml of plasma from ISS patients, yielding approximately 200 µg of exosomes after extraction. For cell culture experiments, we co-cultured 100 µg of these ISS plasma-derived exosomes with 3×10⁵ human C28/I2 chondrocytes in a T25 flask containing 5 ml of culture medium. This setup was used to investigate whether the exosomes inhibit chondrocyte proliferation and markers of endochondral ossification.

Fecal Sample Collection and Storage for miRNA and ELISA Analyses
Fresh fecal samples (2.5 ± 0.5 g) were collected within 30 minutes of defecation using sterile, single-use plastic spoons and transferred into sterile polypropylene containers to prevent contamination. Samples were immediately divided into two aliquots for downstream analyses. For miRNA analysis, one aliquot (~1.5 g) was mixed with RNAlater stabilization solution (1:1 w/v, QIAGEN, Cat No. 76106) and stored at 4°C for 24 hours to ensure RNA stabilization, then transferred to -80°C for long-term storage. For ELISA analysis of inflammatory markers (e.g., IL-1β, TNF-α), a second aliquot (~1 g) was snap-frozen at -80°C without buffer to avoid interference with protein assays. All sample handling was performed using gloves under sterile conditions to minimize contamination.

miRNA and mRNA High-Throughput Sequencing
The miRNA sequencing and data analysis were performed by Shanghai Biotechnology Corporation (Shanghai, China). Briefly, total RNAs were isolated from each sample using the QIAamp RNeasy Serum/Plasma Midi Kit (Cat No. 77044, Qiagen). Subsequently, the sequencing library was constructed with the QIAseq miRNA Library Kit (Cat No. 1103679, Qiagen) and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq platform (California, USA). Differentially expressed miRNAs were identified with P<0.05 and |log2(FC)| ≥ 1.5.

For mRNA analysis, total RNA was extracted using the Eastep® Super RNA easy Kit (Promega, Beijing). Libraries were constructed with the TruSeq Stranded mRNA LT Sample Prep Kit (Illumina). Transcriptome sequencing and differential expression analysis were performed using OE Biotech (Shanghai, China) on an Illumina HiSeq X Ten sequencer. Clean reads were aligned to the human genome using HISAT2, and gene expression levels were quantified via Cufflink and HTSeq-count. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified through fold-change filtering (log2(FC) ≥ 2.0, P<0.05). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment and KEGG pathway analyses were conducted for DEGs and target genes of DE-miRNAs. The miRNA-mRNA regulatory network was visualized based on established methods.

In-Situ Hybridization
Human chondrocytes were incubated with FAM-labeled probes for miR-17-3p for 48 hours at 65°C, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (miRCURY LNA miRNA ISH Kit, Thermo Fisher). The localization of miR-17-3p was visualized using a CY3-labeled sequence (5’-CY3-CTACCTGCACTGTAAGCACTTTG-3’ and 5’-CCACAAGTGCCTTCACTGCAGT-3’, miRCURY LNA miRNA ISH kit, Thermo Fisher, Shanghai, China). Similarly, femur samples from six-week-old rats were decalcified, sectioned, and subjected to in situ hybridization.

Cell Culture, Exosome Isolation, and Extraction of Exosomes from ISS Patient Plasma
The human healthy small intestinal epithelial cell line HIEC-6 (Otwo Biotech, Cat No. HTX1978) and human healthy colon mucosal epithelial cell line NCM460 (Otwo Biotech, Cat. No. HTX1841) were cultured in DMEM enriched with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin, maintained at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. Human chondrocytes C28/I2 (Otwo Biotech, Cat No. HTX2308) were cultured in 89% H-DMEM with 10% FBS in a 37°C incubator with 5% CO2. The hBMSCs were purchased from Otwo Biotech (Shenzhen) Inc. (Cat No. HTX1946) and cultured in an MSC-specific medium, 37°C humidified incubator, 5% CO2 atmosphere. Exosomes were isolated from cell culture media using the Exosome Isolation Kit (Umibio, Cat No. UR52121), and protein quantification was conducted using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Beyotime, Cat No. P0010). Details of Cell culture and exosome isolating methods can be found in our previous publication28.

Cell viability assay
The cell suspension was mixed evenly with 0.4% trypan blue solution (from Beijing Solabao Co., Ltd.) in a 9:1 ratio (final concentration 0.04%). The cells were stained for 3 min, and the cell viability was measured using a cell viability counting instrument (Shanghai Bio-Red Co., Ltd.). Only samples with a cell viability greater than 95% were used for subsequent experiments.

Capsaicin co-culture model with intestinal cells
Natural capsaicin (404-86-4) was purchased from Weilkeqi Co., Ltd. It was dissolved in PBS to prepare a capsaicin solution with an initial concentration of 1 mg/ml. The solution was diluted with complete medium to obtain concentrations of 0 μM, 25 μM, 50 μM, 75 μM, 100 μM, 150 μM, and 200 μM for the intestinal cell (HIEC-6 and NCM460) capsaicin stimulation culture experiments. After a culture period of 0 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h, these cells were used in further experiments.

Cell proliferation assay
The proliferations of chondrocytes, small intestinal epithelial cell line HIEC-6, and human healthy colon mucosal epithelial cell line NCM460 were assessed using the CCK-8 assay (TransGen Biotech). Cells were seeded into 96-well plates and incubated for 24, 48, 72, and 96 hours, followed by absorbance measurements at 450 nm. Additionally, EdU assays (Guangzhou Ribo Bio Co., Ltd. China) were performed to further evaluate cell proliferation of chondrocytes and bmsc, with stained cells imaged via fluorescence microscopy.

Overexpression of miR-17-3p, ZNF148 and SOS1
Overexpression plasmids for miR-17-3p, ZNF148 and SOS1 were constructed by GENEchem Co., Ltd. Cell transfections were carried out using Lipofectamine 3000 (Invitrogen), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Infection efficiency was monitored via microscopy and cells were incubated for 72 h before further experiments. The information for all vectors used in this experiment is presented in Supplementary Fig. 31, Supplementary Fig. 32a, b.

CRISPR-Cas9 knockout system
CRISPR-Cas9 knockdown plasmids targeting ZNF148 and SOS1 for human and rat cells were obtained from Guangzhou VectorBuilder Co., Ltd. (China). Details of the plasmid sequences are provided in Supplementary Fig. 32c–f.

Lentivirus Generation
HEK293T cells were transfected with lentiviral packaging plasmids. Lentiviral supernatants were collected, filtered and concentrated using the Virus Concentration Kit (Beyotime, Cat No. C2901S). The supernatants containing lentiviral particles were extracted and concentrated by a Virus Concentration Kit (Beyotime, C2901S) to a lentiviral stock greater than 1×108 TU/ml (as determined by p24 ELISA), and then frozen at -80°C in PBS solution containing 1% BSA.

C28 Chondrocytes Stable Transfection Strain Construction
All the virus supernatants were prepared using the virus construction methods mentioned in this article. Among them, the titers of overexpression plasmids for miR-17-3p, ZNF148 and SOS1 were greater than 1×109 FU/mL, and the infectious substance concentration (MOI) was 25; the titers of CRISPR-Cas9 knockdown plasmids targeting ZNF148 and SOS1 were greater than 5×108 FU/mL, and the infectious substance concentration (MOI) was 50. Concentrated viral supernatant, mixed with polybrene (8 µg/ml), was used to transfect human chondrocytes in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS. Cells were infected for 48 h and then screened with puromycin for 14 days.

Preparation of miRNA-Loaded Exosomes and Cell Culture Experiments
Exosomes (100 µg) derived from the human chondrocyte cell line C28 were loaded with miRNA (75 µM, ~1 µL) using the ExoFectin® sRNA-into-Exosome Kit (Guangzhou Ribo Bio Co., Ltd., China). The miRNA-17-3p and negative control (NC) mimic sequences were synthesized by Guangzhou Ribo Bio Co., Ltd. (China). The transfected exosomes were harvested using the PureExo® Kit (Cat. #: UR52172, Umbio Co., Ltd., China). Similarly, exosomes (100 µg) isolated from the plasma of ISS patients were loaded with an miRNA-17-3p inhibitor (20 µM, ~1 µL) using the same ExoFectin® sRNA-into-Exosome Kit (Guangzhou Ribo Bio Co., Ltd., China). Details of the preparation of miRNA-loaded exosomes methods can be found in our previous publication57.

For cell culture experiments, 100 µg of ISS plasma-derived exosomes loaded with the miR-17-3p inhibitor were co-cultured with 3×10⁵ human C28/I2 chondrocytes in a T25 flask containing 5 mL of culture medium. This experimental setup was designed to investigate whether suppression of miR-17-3p in ISS plasma exosomes could reverse the inhibition of chondrocyte proliferation and markers of endochondral ossification induced by exosomes of ISS patients.

To evaluate the in vivo effects of miR-17-3p overexpression on height development in immature SD rat, we utilized exosomes derived from primary rat chondrocytes, isolated from the proximal tibia and distal femur growth plates, overexpressing miR-17-3p. The exosome dosage ranged from 200 to 300 µg per injection, determined based on a ratio of 1 µg of exosomes per 0.6 g of rat body weight. Rats were divided into groups at 4 weeks postpartum, and exosomes overexpressing miR-17-3p were injected at weeks 4 and 5, respectively. The experiment was terminated at week 8, and the results were observed.

RT-qPCR and Western blot analysis
RT-qPCR and Western blot methods followed our established protocols. RT-qPCR quantified miRNA and mRNA expression in both cell and tissue samples, using U6 and GAPDH as internal controls. For miRNA RT-qPCR of plasma-derived exosomes and fecal samples, U6 small nuclear RNA was used as the endogenous reference for biological normalization, and its stability across sample types and between ISS and control groups was confirmed using geNorm and NormFinder. An exogenous spike-in (cel-miR-39) was added during RNA extraction to monitor extraction and reverse transcription efficiency, thereby controlling for technical variability. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 2. Reactions were performed in triplicate with three independent cell preparations. Relative expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCt method, with internal controls adjusting for RNA quantity and transcription efficiency.

Protein samples were extracted from harvested chondrocytes and cartilage tissues using a total protein extraction kit (Applygen Technologies Inc.). The BCA assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Inc.) measured total protein concentrations. Protein lysates were separated via SDS-PAGE (Beijing Biosynthesis Biotechnology, Beijing, China) and transferred to PVDF membranes. Membranes were blocked with skim milk (Solarbio Inc.) for 1 h at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation at 4°C with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table 3). After washing with 1× TBST (Solarbio Inc.), membranes were incubated for 1 h at room temperature with HRP-labeled rabbit anti-mouse secondary antibody (1:3000, Abcam, USA). For multiple protein detections, membranes were reprobed with new primary antibodies using WB Stripping buffer (NO: 21059; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Grey values were quantified with Image Lab (v5.2.1).

Von Kossa staining, Alkaline phosphatase staining, and Alizarin Red staining
The Von Kossa staining kit (Shanghai Gefan Biotechnology Co., Ltd), Alkaline Phosphatase Color Development Kit (Solarbio Inc.), and Alizarin Red S solution (Solarbio, G8550) were employed to assess mineralized nodules from chondrocytes in vitro, adhering to the manufacturer’s instructions. Details of the Von Kossa, Alkaline Phosphatase, and Alizarin Red S solution staining methods can be found in our previous publication41,58. Positive calcium nodules appeared as black-brown, dark black, or violet.

Cell cycle profile
A cell cycle analysis kit (KeyGEN BioTECH, China) was used to detect the cell cycle. Chondrocyte (C28) and hBMSC cells were harvested, fixed with 70% ethanol for 2 h at 4°C, and stained with a solution containing propidium iodide (0.05 mg/ml), RNase A (1 mg/ml), and 0.3% Triton X-100 for 30 min in the dark. The percentage of cells in different cell cycle phases was analyzed using a flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA) and ModFIT software, with each experiment repeated three times. The gating strategies for cell cycle analyses are available on Figshare, as indicated in the Data Availability section.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
ELISA kits (Meimian Technology, Jiangsu, China) measured the expression of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-10, Capsaicin, GH, IGF-1, and IGFBP3. Standards and tissue samples (50 μl each) were added to 96-well plates, followed by incubation with HRP-labeled detection antibodies. After incubation, TMB substrate and termination solution were added, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader.

Myeloperoxidase (MPO) and Malondialdehyde (MDA) Activity Assay
MPO activity in intestinal tissues was assessed by homogenizing in saline and measuring absorbance at 460 nm. MDA levels were determined using the MDA Content Assay Kit (Solarbio, China), with absorbance measured at 532 nm.

Luciferase reporter assay
The ZNF148 plasmid or its mutant portions and the miR-17-3p mimic were co-transfected into 293T cells using Lipofiter (Hanbio Biotechnology, Shanghai, China). The Dual-Luciferase Assay System (Promega Corporation) assessed firefly and Renilla luciferase activity 48 hours post-transfection.

ChIP Assay
Chromatin Immunoprecipitation (ChIP) was performed by fixing cells with formaldehyde, lysing them, and fragmenting chromatin via sonication. Specific antibodies of ZNF148 (Santa Cruz, sc-398148X, 200 µg/0.1 ml) were used to immunoprecipitate protein-DNA complexes, followed by washing, reverse crosslinking and DNA purification for subsequent RT-qPCR or ChIP-seq analysis.

Construction of Engineering-target exosomes (ET-exo)
We utilized a membrane fusion protein technique to functionalize the exosome surface with the collagen type II-targeting peptide WYRGRL. This modification enhances specificity for tissues abundant in collagen type II, such as growth plate cartilage and articular cartilage, facilitating targeted exosome delivery. The ET-Exo plasmid, encoding WYRGRL/LAMP2b/EGFP for green fluorescence and GH/mCherry for red fluorescence, was designed and constructed by Vector Builder (Guangzhou, China). The generation of stably transfected cell lines expressing the viral construct and the subsequent exosome isolation were conducted as detailed in the preceding section.

In Vitro and In Vivo bone targeting
To evaluate growth plate targeting in vivo, 4-week-old SD rats (body weight: 150 g) were administered tail vein injections of ET-Exo-si-miR-17-3p-oeGH, normal exosomes, or PBS. Each injection contained exosomes at a concentration of 1 mg in 300 µL, derived from 50 mL of cell supernatant. At predetermined time points, the rats were humanely euthanized, and their bones and organs were harvested for imaging. Fluorescence imaging was performed using an excitation wavelength of 551 nm and an emission wavelength of 567 nm.

Animal feeding and OE-miR-17-3p-rats
The Animal Ethics Committee of Nanchang University approved the experiments (Approval NO: NCULAE-20221031059). The details of all experimental animal groupings are provided in Supplementary Fig. 28. All SD rats were housed individually in cages under standard conditions. Three pregnant rats at 14 days of gestation were purchased and housed individually in three cages with a standard diet for one week until delivery. The details of all experimental animal groupings are provided in Supplementary Fig. 28. All SD rats were housed individually in cages under standard conditions (22±2°C, 50–60% relative humidity, 12 h light/dark cycle) and fed a mixed diet (AIN-93, Beijing Keao Xieli Feed Company). Eighteen pregnant rats at 14 days of gestation were purchased and housed individually in 18 cages with a standard AIN-93 diet, maintained for one week until delivery. Each pregnant rat typically produced 10-14 pups, and after three weeks post-birth—when sex could be visually identified—pups underwent the first random allocation. To clarify whether miR-17-3p exerts biological effects through ZNF148/SOS1 in vivo experiments, 4 male SD rats were randomly selected from each of the 6 litters and divided into 4 groups at random. They were housed in 4 cages, with 6 male SD rats per cage, under standard conditions and fed the AIN-93 diet. The miR-17-3p, ZNF148, and SOS1 plasmids (GV367-Ubi-MCS-SV40-EGFP-IRES-puromycin) were constructed by GENEchem Co., Ltd. In group A (n=6), the 300 µL PBS was injected into the tail vein. The miR-17-3p was overexpressed in 3 week rats via tail-vein injection in groups B to D. After the rats reached 4 weeks of age, these rats received injections via the tail vein every 3 days, with Group B (n=6) receiving 300 µl of PBS, with Group C (n=6) receiving 300 µl of ZNF148 plasmid, and Group D (n=6) receiving 300 µl of SOS1 plasmid (Supplementary Fig. 28a). To clarify the biological role of ET-Exos from chondrocytes in in vivo experiments, 6 male SD rats were randomly selected from 6 litters and divided into 6 groups at random. They were housed in 6 cages, with 6 male SD rats per cage, under standard conditions and fed the AIN-93 diet. In group A (n=6), the 300 µL PBS was injected into the tail vein. The miR-17-3p was overexpressed in 3-week-old rats via tail-vein injection in groups B to E. After the rats reached 4 weeks of age, these rats received injections via the tail vein every 3 days, with Group B (n=6) receiving 300 µl of ET-Exos (si-miR-17-3p+GH), Group C (n=6) receiving 300 µl of Exos (si-miR-17-3p+GH), Group D (n=6) receiving 300 µl of PBS, Group E (n=6) receiving 300 µl of Exos (si-miR-17-3p), and Group F (n=6) receiving 300 µl of Exos (GH) (Supplementary Fig. 28b). Furthermore, we employed the same methods and protocols to evaluate the in vivo biological effects of ET exosomes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (Supplementary Fig. 29a). The body weight and height of rats were recorded weekly, with measurements continuing for four weeks. At the end of the 8-week experimental period, the rats were euthanized using a standard method involving CO2 asphyxiation, in accordance with institutional animal care guidelines. Knee joint tissue samples were then collected for analysis of cartilage growth and development. Height and weight analyses were conducted as single-blind assessments to minimize bias.

Safranin O and Fast Green staining and Calcein staining
For all samples in this research, one-third of the distal femur was resected and kept in 4% formaldehyde solution. 4 µm thickness, serial sections were obtained for Safranin O/Fast Green staining and calcein staining. The flow chart (Figure S10, Supporting Information) demonstrates the detailed grouping information. Details of Safranin O/Fast Green staining and calcein staining methods can be found in our previous publication41,59,60.

Immunofluorescence Staining
4 μm paraffin sections were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to antigen retrieval in sodium citrate buffer. Following PBS washes, sections were blocked with 3% BSA for 30 min at room temperature, then incubated with 3% H2O2 and 5% goat serum to block nonspecific binding. Primary antibodies (Col10a1, Runx2, Opn, Ocn, Sos1, Znf148, Ras, Pi3k, p-Pi3k, Akt, p-Akt, Erk1/2, p-Erk1/2) were applied overnight, followed by secondary antibodies (1:200 dilution). Nuclei were stained with DAPI, and images were captured using fluorescence microscopy. Image-Pro Plus 6.0 software was used for analysis.

Explant Culture of Neonatal SD Rat Femurs with miR-17-3p Overexpression and Znf148/Sos1 Knockdown
Approval for the use of rat limbs was obtained from the Animal Ethics Committee of Nanchang University. Femurs from neonatal SD rats were harvested one day postpartum. The harvested tissues were cultured statically in BGJb medium (Gibco, Australia) supplemented with 6 mg/ml bovine serum albumin (BSA; Gibco, Australia), 150 µg/ml ascorbic acid (Solarbio, Cat: A8100), 100 units/ml penicillin, and 100 µg/ml streptomycin (Gibco, Australia). Cultures were maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2, and the medium, replenished with fresh reagents, was replaced daily.

For gene editing and overexpression studies, CRISPR-Cas9 knockdown plasmids targeting Znf148 and Sos1 and an miR-17-3p overexpression plasmid were acquired from Guangzhou VectorBuilder Co., Ltd. and GENEchem Co., Ltd (China). Detailed plasmid sequence information is provided in Supplementary Fig. 31c–f. To generate lentiviral particles, HEK293T cells were transfected with lentiviral packaging plasmids corresponding to the knockdown and overexpression constructs. The resulting lentiviral supernatants were collected, filtered, and concentrated using a Virus Concentration Kit (Beyotime, Cat: C2901S). The concentrated supernatants, containing lentiviral particles, achieved a titer greater than 1×10^8 TU/ml (as quantified by p24 ELISA) and were stored at –80°C in PBS supplemented with 1% BSA.

For transfection of the neonatal rat growth plate tissue, a 2 ml culture system in a 24-well plate was used. The concentrated lentiviral supernatant (titer >5×10^8 FU/ml, multiplicity of infection [MOI]=200) was combined with 8 µg/ml polybrene and HiTransGA (Genechem Co., Ltd., Shanghai), a specialized viral transfection reagent, to facilitate efficient transduction. The tissue was cultured in fresh medium during transfection with lentiviral particles carrying either the Znf148/Sos1 knockdown constructs or the miR-17-3p overexpression construct. The medium was replaced 72 hours post-transfection and refreshed daily thereafter. After 14 days of culture, samples were analyzed using RT-qPCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence. Details of the in vitro experimental groupings are provided in Supplementary Fig. 30.

Isolation of primary chondrocytes from the growth plate of neonatal SD rats
Primary chondrocytes were isolated from the growth plate of one-week-old neonatal SD rats. The rats were euthanized with isoflurane, disinfected with 75% ethanol for 30 min, wiped with iodophor three times, and rinsed with pre-cooled PBS. The upper segments of the bilateral tibia and lower segments of the femur were dissected, and the cartilage was cut into ~1 mm³ fragments. These fragments were washed three times with PBS to remove blood cells.

The cartilage fragments were first digested with 0.25% trypsin at 37°C for 20 min to remove fibers and impurities, then centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was washed with PBS. The pellet was further digested with 0.2% type II collagenase (filtered and sterilized) at 37°C for 4 h with gentle shaking every 30 minutes until fully dissolved. Digestion was stopped with DMEM/F12 medium, and the cell suspension was filtered through a 40 µm cell sieve. The filtrate was centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, the supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was washed with PBS. The isolated chondrocytes were cultured in DMEM/F12 medium with 50 µg/mL ascorbic acid. The medium was changed every 2–3 days to remove unattached cells, retaining adherent chondrocytes for experiments.

Capsaicin animal model
All SD rats were housed individually under standard conditions. Three pregnant rats at 14 days of gestation were purchased and housed individually in three cages with a standard diet for one week until delivery. The details of all experimental animal groupings are provided in Supplementary Fig. 28. All SD rats were housed individually under standard conditions. Three pregnant rats at 14 days of gestation were purchased and housed individually in three cages with a standard diet for one week until delivery. Each pregnant rat produced 4 male and 4 female pups, yielding a total of 24 offspring. At three weeks post-birth, 4 male and 4 female pups from each litter were selected and housed individually, followed by one week on a capsaicin-free diet. For group allocation, from each litter, 2 males and 2 females were randomly assigned to the capsaicin-supplemented diet group and the remaining 2 males and 2 females were assigned to the control group. Beginning in the fourth week, the 24 rats were distributed into eight cages for further rearing. Four cages, each containing three rats (12 rats in total: 6 males and 6 females), were maintained on a capsaicin-free diet, while the other four cages (also 12 rats in total: 6 males and 6 females) were switched to a capsaicin-supplemented diet. Thus, both the control and capsaicin groups consisted of 6 males and 6 females. Food intake data were measured every two days, and body weight and height were recorded weekly, by calculating the difference between the amount of food provided and the remaining food, with measurements continuing for four weeks. At the end of the 8-week experimental period, the rats were euthanized using a standard method involving CO2 asphyxiation, in accordance with institutional animal care guidelines. Knee joint and intestinal tissue samples were then collected for analysis of cartilage growth and development as well as gut inflammation-related parameters. Height, weight, food intake, and intestinal tissue inflammation analyses were conducted as single-blind assessments to minimize bias.

The information on the diet composition and form shown in Supplemental Table 4. The standard AIN-93 diet is the unmodified AIN-93G chow, while the capsaicin-supplemented diet is the AIN-93G formulation with 0.01% (w/w) capsaicin incorporated. The capsaicin-supplemented diet was purchased from Ke’ao Synergy (Tianjin) Feed Co., Ltd., Tianjin, China. To ensure accuracy, we verified the capsaicin concentration using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), confirming a consistent 0.01% (w/w) level with a variation of less than 5%. For more details, please refer to the information in the Supplementary Fig. 29b.

The small intestinal samples were collected at 10 cm and 40 cm from the pylorus, while colonic samples were taken at 5 cm and 10 cm from the anus. Each segment was 4 cm in length, with 1 cm was fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 5 μm thickness, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for histological analysis to assess mucosal stimulation and inflammation, and the remaining 3 cm utilized for Western blot and RT-qPCR analyses to evaluate molecular changes. Villus height and wall thickness of intestinal and colon were measured in 5-6 random fields per section under a light microscope (Olympus BX53, Japan) at 20× magnification using Image-Pro Plus 6.0 software. Villus height was determined from the villus tip to the crypt-villus junction, and intestinal wall thickness was measured from the mucosa to the serosa. Data were averaged per segment per rat, and mean values for the capsaicin and control groups were compared for each intestinal region (small intestine and colon) using Student’s t-test (p<0.05 considered significant).

Capsaicin dose selection and physiological relevance
To model physiologically relevant dietary capsaicin exposure observed in high-consumption populations—particularly those in Jiangxi and Sichuan provinces, China—a 0.01% (w/w) capsaicin-supplemented diet was administered to 4-week-old SD rats, representing the juvenile growth stage.

Capsaicin concentrations in six typical Jiangxi dishes, sourced from local restaurants, were determined by HPLC, ranging from 0.0025 to 0.6277 mg/g (mean±SD=0.2181±0.2400 mg/g). These values are consistent with those reported by Jia et al.61, who identified mean capsaicinoid concentrations of 0.1756 mg/g (grade 4) and 0.2076 mg/g (grade 5) in Sichuan dishes—levels that are common in Jiangxi diets. Assuming a 70 kg adult consumes 700 g/day of grade 4–5 dishes, the estimated capsaicin intake is 122.9–145.3 mg/day (1.76–2.08 mg/kg/day); for a 40 kg adolescent consuming 400 g/day, the intake is 70.2–83.0 mg/day (1.76–2.08 mg/kg/day).

In this study, 4-week-old SD rats (average weight ≈ 70 g) consumed 7.5 g/day of a 0.01% capsaicin-supplemented diet, with capsaicin concentration verified by HPLC, resulting in an intake of 0.75 mg/day (10.71 mg/kg/day). Based on body-surface-area normalization (FDA, 2005) and a rat-to-human conversion factor of 6.2, the human equivalent dose (HED) was calculated to be approximately 1.73 mg/kg/day—closely aligning with the estimated intake among Jiangxi residents. Furthermore, Martínez-Aceviz et al.62 reported a mean capsaicin intake of 152.4 mg/day (2.18 mg/kg/day for a 70 kg adult) in Tijuana, Mexico, further supporting the global relevance of our dosing strategy for modeling high-consumption populations.

Histopathological analysis
Colon tissues were fixed in 10% paraformaldehyde, paraffin-embedded, sectioned (10 μm), and stained with H&E. Two pathologists independently scored the samples under a light microscope.

Apoptosis assays
For the apoptosis assays, cells (5×10⁵) were seeded and exposed to a range of capsaicin concentrations (0–200 μM) for 72 hours. After trypsinization, the cells were stained with Annexin V FITC/PI and analyzed via flow cytometry using FlowJo software. The gating strategies for apoptosis analyses are available on Figshare, as indicated in the Data Availability section. These experiments were conducted independently three times, with each concentration tested in triplicate per experiment to ensure robust statistical reliability.

RNA extraction from Stool and Blood
Total RNA was isolated from stool and blood samples using commercial kits (Solarbio, R1290; Tiangen, DP443). Total RNA from fecal and plasma samples was quantified and purity-assessed using an ultra-micro ultraviolet-visible spectrophotometer (ND-100C, MIU-LAB, China).

High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC)
The high-performance liquid chromatography system (WATER-E2695) was used. The chromatographic column was [column model, such as Agilent ZORBAX Eclipse Plus C18, 4.6×150 mm, 3.5 μm], and the column temperature was set at 30°C. The mobile phase consisted of phase A (ultrapure water) and phase B (methanol), with gradient elution. The flow rate was 1.0 mL/min and the injection volume was 20 μL. The detection wavelength was set at 280 nm. The standard curve was set with concentrations of 0.05, 2, 10, 20, and 200 ug/ml (Supplementary Fig. 26).

Statistical analysis
The data distribution was assessed prior to analysis using the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality. Parametric tests (Student’s t-test for two-group comparisons and one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple groups) were employed when data followed a normal distribution, as confirmed in all cases. If non-normality had been detected, non-parametric alternatives (e.g., Mann-Whitney U test for two groups and Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc for multiple groups) would have been used; however, this was not necessary. The diagnostic efficacy of miR-17-3p was evaluated through ROC curve analysis utilizing the Xiantao platform. All statistical tests were conducted using GraphPad software (10.1.2 version). P-values of less than 0.001 (***), 0.01 (**), and 0.05 (*) were deemed statistically significant. Not significant was ns.

Title: “Capsaicin Diet-Induced Gut Inflammation Elevates Plasma Exosomal miR-17-3p: Unveiling the ZNF148/SOS1 Axis
as a Novel Mechanism in ISS Pathogenesis and Potential Therapeutic Target”
Authors: Professor Jia and colleagues
This manuscript presents an impressive, comprehensive, and highly innovative study, spanning from clinical observations in
children with idiopathic short stature (ISS) to sophisticated experimental work using animal models, tissue cultures, and cell
cultures. Employing a wide range of state-of-the-art methodologies, the authors provide compelling results that are well-
presented and of significant clinical relevance.
To enhance the clarity and accessibility of the findings, I recommend the inclusion of a graphical summary to provide a
visual overview of the study's key components and outcomes.
The study makes a novel contribution to our understanding of the mechanisms underlying growth faltering in children, an
area where clinicians often lack effective therapeutic options. The introduction effectively sets the stage by addressing the
challenges associated with ISS, including the unknown etiology and the limited access to recombinant human growth
hormone (rhGH) therapy in many regions due to high costs and limited insurance coverage. While the authors highlight the
risks associated with rhGH therapy, it is important to acknowledge that these side effects are rare. For example, studies such
as Savendhal et al. (J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2021) and Cianfarani (Front Endocrinol, 2021) support the safety profile of
rhGH. Providing quantitative data on the incidence of side effects would offer a more balanced perspective. Additionally, the
statement that ISS "seriously affects the physical and mental health of children" should be rephrased to avoid
overgeneralization.
The study’s insights into the role of subclinical inflammation in ISS, particularly in specific
regions of China, have broader implications. Previous work, such as Menahem et al. (Nutrients, 2023), highlights the
potential for dietary interventions to mitigate growth attenuation due to LPS induced inflammation, further supporting the authors' conclusions. Moreover, the development of
exosome-based therapeutic strategies targeting the growth plate is highly promising and could
revolutionize ISS treatment.

hypothesized to reduce microbial growth and thus reduce gut inflammation and diarrhea - therefore it is worth further
